translations: One of the little fish couldn't help but pipe up, "Aman, your brushstrokes look like you're painting bubbles!" Another little fish chimed in, laughing, "Why don't we help you change the character for 'mouth' to 'wind'?" Aman couldn't help but chuckle, patting his chest and saying, "That's a great idea! If the wind blows my writing away, my records will be even more carefree!"

He gently lifted the tip of his brush, took a deep breath of the sea air, and made a mental note: whether he was writing about the "seaside" or the "edge of the sky," it was all just an excuse, especially with the giant bird, transformed from the massive Kun fish, blurring the lines between heaven and earth right before his eyes.

Just then, the giant bird spread its wings, its feathers like clouds, stretching towards the sky. The June winds rose from the sea surface, whipping up waves and ripples, as if trying to lift the entire North Sea. Aman's bamboo slips were lifted by the gentle breeze, the pages trembling in the wind, but he held them tightly in place.

He muttered to himself, "This wind is really taking my brush to new heights!" He then stopped his brush on the last character, writing an incomplete sentence, leaving it for the little fish to ponder later.

A little fish asked from behind the waves, "Is this bamboo slip enough?" Aman looked up, smiling and nodding, his eyes reflecting the magnificent sight of the giant bird riding the June winds, its wings like clouds, carrying the blue sky, and flying effortlessly towards the South Sea Heaven Pool.
A little fish asked from behind the waves, "Is this bamboo slip enough?"
He replied, "Enough to write 'not enough'."

The strong winds reached the bird's wings. Instead of flapping them forcefully like before, the bird lifted its wings to ride the wind. The wind supported it, first lifting it off the cliff, then over the sea surface.

At first, the bird could still see every rocky outcropping on the shore. As the wind continued to lift it, those familiar perches grew smaller. The bird didn't panic and fold its wings; instead, it kept them in a position where the wind could support it, making its ascent a continuous motion.

The North Sea responded with long waves, but they weren't just an echo of the bird's futile struggles. The bird's body truly rose, the cliffs receding below, and the sea surface, once endless, gradually revealed its full contours.

The old brush almost slipped from his hand. He quickly gripped it tightly, remembering the page in "The Twenty Bamboo Slips of Mountains and Seas" about the Eight Immortals crossing the sea. He whispered, "Last time, the winds and waves were only in the sea. This time, the North Sea seems to have given the winds and waves wings."

He said no more. The bird's takeoff wasn't a spectacle for the historian to behold, nor did it need a single word of explanation from the shore. He simply protected the old brush and watched in silence.

The giant bird continued to rise, riding the June winds. The clouds parted, and the sky's light fell upon its feathers. It didn't return to the water or circle above the North Sea, showing off. It had been waiting for this wind all along, and its purpose was to leave.

The small birds flew out from behind the rocks, trying to follow the giant bird for a while. They rose quickly on the strong winds but soon stopped at the familiar mountain peaks. The lead bird watched as the giant bird disappeared into the distance, saying, "It wasn't waiting for the winds to start its wings."
Another bird asked, "What was it waiting for?"
"The wind that turns the distance into a path."

The fish in the water chased after the bird's shadow, swimming until the reefs blocked their way. The fish that had once called the Kun fish a "moving mountain" finally admitted, "This time, it's not the mountain that's moving."
Its companion asked, "What is it, then?"
The fish thought for a while before saying, "It's the sky with a new path, and we can't swim up to it."

The giant bird carried the blue sky on its back, its wings supported by the wind. The fish in the North Sea looked up to see only a moving cloud shadow. The "moving mountain" had left the water, becoming a truly distant-flying giant bird.

Aman waited until the bird's shadow had crossed the North Sea's edge before picking up his brush again. He didn't decide the bird's destination; he simply wrote what he had seen: the giant bird riding the June winds, its wings like clouds, flying south. After finishing, he tucked the old brush into the green bamboo slips, lest the last gust of wind blow his records away.
The bird rode the June winds, taking no orders from anyone, nor completing any task for others. The South Sea Heaven Pool waited in the distance, and the bird had set its own course.

The giant bird flew over the North Sea, heading towards the South Sea Heaven Pool. Behind it was the deep water it had lived in, and ahead was the unknown heaven and earth; this long-awaited journey had finally crossed the North Sea's boundaries.

After leaving the North Sea, the giant bird flew over the clouds for a long time. The June winds continued to blow from beneath its wings, and it didn't need to flap them every time; it only adjusted its direction when the wind changed.

At first, the North Sea was like a vast, clear mirror behind it. Later, mountains and rivers appeared, and the fish's lifelong reef, once a massive obstruction, became just a small dark shadow on the water's edge from up high.

The giant bird didn't think the things below were unimportant just because they had grown smaller. It was these rivers, valleys, and the lives within them that gave its journey meaning. The bird just no longer considered any one place the entirety of the world.
A flock of migratory birds, carried by the wind, saw the giant bird and asked where it was headed.
"The South Sea Heaven Pool."
The migratory birds said, "There's a lake not far from here, with clear water, plenty of fish, and a shore where you can take shelter from the wind."
The giant bird thanked them but didn't change course.
